Chapter 11-Vectors.question_text: With the same square and notation as in 2a, find $\overrightarrow{BE}$ in terms of $\mathbf{b}$ and $\mathbf{d}$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.hint: Use position vectors: take $A$ as origin, so $B$ has position $\mathbf{b}$, $D$ has $\mathbf{d}$ and $E$ is the centre of the square at $\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{d}$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.solution_text: If $\vec{OA}=\mathbf{0}$, then $\vec{OB}=\mathbf{b}$ and $\vec{OD}=\mathbf{d}$. The square has side vectors $2\mathbf{b}$ and $2\mathbf{d}$, so the centre $E$ has position $\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{d}$. Thus $\overrightarrow{BE}=\vec{OE}-\vec{OB}=(\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{d})-\mathbf{b}=\mathbf{d}$.

Chapter 11-Vectors.question_text: Find $\overrightarrow{HG}$ in terms of $\mathbf{b}$ and $\mathbf{d}$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.hint: Use positions of $H$ and $G$ as midpoints on right side and top-right corner.
Chapter 11-Vectors.solution_text: $G$ is top-right corner, so $\vec{OG}=2\mathbf{b}+2\mathbf{d}$. $H$ is midpoint of $GI$, where $\vec{OI}=2\mathbf{d}$, so $\vec{OH}=\dfrac{\vec{OG}+\vec{OI}}{2}=\dfrac{(2\mathbf{b}+2\mathbf{d})+2\mathbf{d}}{2}=\mathbf{b}+2\mathbf{d}$. Hence $\overrightarrow{HG}=\vec{OG}-\vec{OH}=(2\mathbf{b}+2\mathbf{d})-(\mathbf{b}+2\mathbf{d})=\mathbf{b}$.

Chapter 11-Vectors.question_text: Find $\overrightarrow{DF}$ in terms of $\mathbf{b}$ and $\mathbf{d}$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.hint: Use positions of $D$ (midpoint of $AI$) and $F$ (midpoint of $CG$).
Chapter 11-Vectors.solution_text: $\vec{OD}=\mathbf{d}$. $C$ is top-left, so $\vec{OC}=2\mathbf{b}$; $G$ is $2\mathbf{b}+2\mathbf{d}$, so midpoint $F$ has $\vec{OF}=\dfrac{\vec{OC}+\vec{OG}}{2}=\dfrac{2\mathbf{b}+(2\mathbf{b}+2\mathbf{d})}{2}=2\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{d}$. Thus $\overrightarrow{DF}=\vec{OF}-\vec{OD}=(2\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{d})-\mathbf{d}=2\mathbf{b}$.

Vectors $\mathbf{p}$ and $\mathbf{m}$ are equal to $\overrightarrow{OP}$ and $\overrightarrow{OM}$ respectively. Express $\overrightarrow{OA}$ in terms of $\mathbf{p}$ and $\mathbf{m}$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.hint: Use that $M$ is midpoint of $OA$, so $\overrightarrow{OM}$ is half of $\overrightarrow{OA}$.

Express $\overrightarrow{BN}$ in terms of $\mathbf{p}$ and $\mathbf{m}$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.hint: Find position vectors of $B$ and $N$; $N$ is midpoint of $BC$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.solution_text: In the parallelogram, $\overrightarrow{OA}=2\mathbf{m}$ and $\overrightarrow{OB}=2\mathbf{p}$, so $\vec{OC}=\vec{OA}+\vec{OB}=2\mathbf{m}+2\mathbf{p}$. As $N$ is midpoint of $BC$, $\vec{ON}=\dfrac{\vec{OB}+\vec{OC}}{2}=\dfrac{2\mathbf{p}+(2\mathbf{m}+2\mathbf{p})}{2}=\mathbf{m}+2\mathbf{p}$. Then $\overrightarrow{BN}=\vec{ON}-\vec{OB}=(\mathbf{m}+2\mathbf{p})-2\mathbf{p}=\mathbf{m}$.

Chapter 11-Vectors.question_text: Express $\overrightarrow{DQ}$ in terms of $\mathbf{p}$ and $\mathbf{m}$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.hint: Use that $D$ is the intersection of $MN$ and $PQ$ in the midpoint parallelogram, so $D$ is their midpoint.
Chapter 11-Vectors.solution_text: $M$ has $\vec{OM}=\mathbf{m}$, $N$ has $\vec{ON}=\mathbf{m}+2\mathbf{p}$, $P$ has $\vec{OP}=\mathbf{p}$, and $Q$ has $\vec{OQ}=2\mathbf{m}+\mathbf{p}$. Lines $MN$ and $PQ$ are diagonals of the midpoint parallelogram, so $D$ is their midpoint: $\vec{OD}=\dfrac{\vec{OM}+\vec{ON}}{2}=\dfrac{\mathbf{m}+(\mathbf{m}+2\mathbf{p})}{2}=\mathbf{m}+\mathbf{p}$. Then $\overrightarrow{DQ}=\vec{OQ}-\vec{OD}=(2\mathbf{m}+\mathbf{p})-(\mathbf{m}+\mathbf{p})=\mathbf{m}$.

$ABCD$ is a trapezium with $AB\parallel DC$ and $DC=3AB$. $M$ divides $DC$ such that $DM:MC=2:1$. $\overrightarrow{AB}=a$ and $\overrightarrow{BC}=b$. Find $\overrightarrow{AM}$ in terms of $a$ and $b$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.hint: Take $A$ as origin so $\vec{A}=\mathbf{0}$, then write position vectors of $B,C,D,M$ and subtract.
Chapter 11-Vectors.solution_text: Take $\vec{A}=\mathbf{0}$. Then $\vec{B}=a$. Also $\vec{C}=\vec{B}+\vec{BC}=a+b$. Since $\vec{DC}=3\vec{AB}=3a$, we have $\vec{D}=\vec{C}-3a=(a+b)-3a=-2a+b$. On $DC$, $DM:MC=2:1$ so $\vec{M}=\vec{D}+\dfrac{2}{3}(\vec{C}-\vec{D})$. But $\vec{C}-\vec{D}=3a$, hence $\vec{M}=(-2a+b)+\dfrac{2}{3}(3a)=-2a+b+2a=b$. Therefore $\overrightarrow{AM}=\vec{M}-\vec{A}=b$.

Chapter 11-Vectors.question_text: Given $a=\begin{pmatrix}p\\-q\end{pmatrix},\ b=\begin{pmatrix}q\\p\end{pmatrix},\ c=\begin{pmatrix}7\\4\end{pmatrix}$ and $a+2b=c$, find $p$ and $q$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.hint: Compute $a+2b$ and equate components with $c$ to get two simultaneous equations.
Chapter 11-Vectors.solution_text: $a+2b=\begin{pmatrix}p\\-q\end{pmatrix}+2\begin{pmatrix}q\\p\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}p+2q\\-q+2p\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}7\\4\end{pmatrix}$. Hence $p+2q=7$ and $2p-q=4$. From $p+2q=7$ we get $p=7-2q$. Substitute into $2p-q=4$: $2(7-2q)-q=4\Rightarrow14-4q-q=4\Rightarrow14-5q=4\Rightarrow-5q=-10\Rightarrow q=2$, then $p=7-2\cdot2=3$.So $p=3,\ q=2.$ So $p=3,\ q=2.$

Chapter 11-Vectors.question_text: The position vectors of three vertices of a parallelogram are $\begin{pmatrix}4\\2\end{pmatrix}$, $\begin{pmatrix}3\\5\end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix}8\\6\end{pmatrix}$. Find the possible position vectors of the fourth vertex.
Chapter 11-Vectors.hint: Use the fact that for a parallelogram the sum of opposite vertices (position vectors) is equal: if $p,q,r$ are three vertices and $s$ is the fourth, then $s=q+r-p$ or $s=p+r-q$ or $s=p+q-r$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.solution_text: Let $p=\begin{pmatrix}4\\2\end{pmatrix},\ q=\begin{pmatrix}3\\5\end{pmatrix},\ r=\begin{pmatrix}8\\6\end{pmatrix}$. Possible fourth vertices correspond to choosing which given vertex is opposite the unknown: (i) if $s$ is opposite $p$, then $s=q+r-p=\begin{pmatrix}3\\5\end{pmatrix}+\begin{pmatrix}8\\6\end{pmatrix}-\begin{pmatrix}4\\2\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}7\\9\end{pmatrix}$; (ii) if $s$ is opposite $q$, then $s=p+r-q=\begin{pmatrix}4\\2\end{pmatrix}+\begin{pmatrix}8\\6\end{pmatrix}-\begin{pmatrix}3\\5\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}9\\3\end{pmatrix}$; (iii) if $s$ is opposite $r$, then $s=p+q-r=\begin{pmatrix}4\\2\end{pmatrix}+\begin{pmatrix}3\\5\end{pmatrix}-\begin{pmatrix}8\\6\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\1\end{pmatrix}$. So the possible position vectors of the fourth vertex are $\begin{pmatrix}7\\9\end{pmatrix}$, $\begin{pmatrix}9\\3\end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix}-1\\1\end{pmatrix}$.

Chapter 11-Vectors.question_text: Given that the point $A$ has position vector $4\mathbf{i}-5\mathbf{j}$ and the point $B$ has position vector $6\mathbf{i}+3\mathbf{j}$, find the vector $\overrightarrow{AB}$.
With $A(4\mathbf{i}-5\mathbf{j})$ and $B(6\mathbf{i}+3\mathbf{j})$, find $|\overrightarrow{AB}|$ giving your answer as a simplified surd.
$A$ lies on the circle $x^{2}+y^{2}=9$. Given that $\overrightarrow{OA}=2k\mathbf{i}+k\mathbf{j}$, find the exact value of $k$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.hint: Substitute $(x,y)=(2k,k)$ into $x^{2}+y^{2}=9$ to form an equation in $k$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.solution_text: Since $A$ is $(2k,k)$ we have $(2k)^{2}+k^{2}=9\Rightarrow4k^{2}+k^{2}=5k^{2}=9\Rightarrow k^{2}=\dfrac{9}{5}$. Thus $k=\pm\dfrac{3}{\sqrt5}=\pm\dfrac{3\sqrt5}{5}.$

Chapter 11-Vectors.question_text: The point $B$ lies on the line with equation $2y=12-3x$. Given that $|OB|=\sqrt{13}$, find possible expressions for $\overrightarrow{OB}$ in the form $p\mathbf{i}+q\mathbf{j}$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.hint: Use line equation $y=(12-3x)/2$ together with circle equation $x^{2}+y^{2}=13$, then solve the resulting quadratic for $x$ and find corresponding $y$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.solution_text: On the line $2y=12-3x$ we have $y=\dfrac{12-3x}{2}$. Because $|OB|=\sqrt{13}$, coordinates $(x,y)$ satisfy $x^{2}+y^{2}=13$. Substitute: $$x^{2}+\left(\dfrac{12-3x}{2}\right)^{2}=13.$$ Then $$x^{2}+\dfrac{(12-3x)^{2}}{4}=13\Rightarrow4x^{2}+(12-3x)^{2}=52\Rightarrow4x^{2}+144-72x+9x^{2}=52,$$ $$13x^{2}-72x+92=0.$$ Solving, $$x=\dfrac{72\pm\sqrt{72^{2}-4\cdot13\cdot92}}{2\cdot13}=\dfrac{72\pm\sqrt{5184-4784}}{26}=\dfrac{72\pm20}{26},$$ so $x=2$ or $x=\dfrac{46}{13}$. For $x=2$, $y=\dfrac{12-3\cdot2}{2}=\dfrac{6}{2}=3$, giving $\overrightarrow{OB}=2\mathbf{i}+3\mathbf{j}$. For $x=\dfrac{46}{13}$, $y=\dfrac{12-3\cdot\frac{46}{13}}{2}=\dfrac{12-\frac{138}{13}}{2}=\dfrac{\frac{156-138}{13}}{2}=\dfrac{\frac{18}{13}}{2}=\dfrac{9}{13}$, giving $\overrightarrow{OB}=\dfrac{46}{13}\mathbf{i}+\dfrac{9}{13}\mathbf{j}$. Thus the possible expressions are $2\mathbf{i}+3\mathbf{j}$ and $\dfrac{46}{13}\mathbf{i}+\dfrac{9}{13}\mathbf{j}$.

Chapter 11-Vectors.question_text: In the diagram, $\overrightarrow{WX}=a$, $\overrightarrow{WY}=b$ and $\overrightarrow{WZ}=c$, and it is given that $\overrightarrow{XY}=\overrightarrow{YZ}$. Prove that $a+c=2b$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.hint: Write $\overrightarrow{XY}$ and $\overrightarrow{YZ}$ in terms of $a,b,c$ and use $\overrightarrow{XY}=\overrightarrow{YZ}$.

Chapter 11-Vectors.question_text: $OAB$ is a triangle. $P,Q,R$ are the midpoints of $OA,AB,OB$ respectively. $\overrightarrow{OP}=p$ and $\overrightarrow{OR}=r$. Find $\overrightarrow{OB}$ in terms of $p$ and $r$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.hint: Use the fact that $P$ and $R$ are midpoints so $OP=\tfrac12 OA$ and $OR=\tfrac12 OB$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.solution_text: Since $P$ is the midpoint of $OA$, $\overrightarrow{OP}=\tfrac12\overrightarrow{OA}$ so $p=\tfrac12\overrightarrow{OA}\Rightarrow\overrightarrow{OA}=2p.$ Similarly $R$ is the midpoint of $OB$, so $r=\tfrac12\overrightarrow{OB}\Rightarrow\overrightarrow{OB}=2r.$

Chapter 11-Vectors.question_text: With the same triangle as in 2a-i, find $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ in terms of $p$ and $r$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.hint: First find $\overrightarrow{OQ}$ using the midpoint of $AB$, then use $\overrightarrow{PQ}=\overrightarrow{OQ}-\overrightarrow{OP}$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.solution_text: Since $Q$ is the midpoint of $AB$, $\overrightarrow{OQ}=\tfrac12(\overrightarrow{OA}+\overrightarrow{OB})=\tfrac12(2p+2r)=p+r.$ Then $\overrightarrow{PQ}=\overrightarrow{OQ}-\overrightarrow{OP}=(p+r)-p=r.$

Chapter 11-Vectors.question_text: Hence prove that triangle $PAQ$ is similar to triangle $OAB$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.hint: Express the side vectors of both triangles in terms of $p$ and $r$ and compare them.
Chapter 11-Vectors.solution_text: For $\triangle OAB$: $\overrightarrow{OA}=2p,\ \overrightarrow{OB}=2r,\ \overrightarrow{AB}=\overrightarrow{OB}-\overrightarrow{OA}=2r-2p=2(r-p).$ For $\triangle PAQ$: $\overrightarrow{PA}=\overrightarrow{OA}-\overrightarrow{OP}=2p-p=p,\ \overrightarrow{PQ}=r$ (from part a-ii), and $\overrightarrow{AQ}=\overrightarrow{OQ}-\overrightarrow{OA}=(p+r)-2p=r-p.$ Thus the three corresponding sides of $\triangle PAQ$ are $p,r,r-p$, which are each exactly half of the corresponding sides $2p,2r,2(r-p)$ of $\triangle OAB$. Therefore all corresponding side lengths are in the ratio $1:2$ and the included angles are equal, so $\triangle PAQ\sim\triangle OAB.$

Chapter 11-Vectors.question_text: $OAB$ is a triangle with $\overrightarrow{OA}=a$ and $\overrightarrow{OB}=b$. The point $M$ divides $OA$ in the ratio $2:1$ and $MN$ is parallel to $OB$. Express the vector $\overrightarrow{ON}$ in terms of $a$ and $b$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.hint: Use the fact that $M$ is on $OA$ and similar triangles $AMN$ and $AOB$ (since $MN\parallel OB$) to find $AN$ as a fraction of $AB$, then obtain $ON=OA+AN$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.solution_text: Since $M$ divides $OA$ in the ratio $2:1$, taking $OM:MA=2:1$ gives $OM=\tfrac23 a$ and $AM=\tfrac13 a.$ Because $MN\parallel OB$, $\triangle AMN\sim\triangle AOB$ with scale factor $k=AM/AO=(\tfrac13 a)/a=\tfrac13.$ Hence $AN=k\cdot AB=\tfrac13(b-a).$ Therefore $\overrightarrow{ON}=\overrightarrow{OA}+\overrightarrow{AN}=a+\tfrac13(b-a)=a+\tfrac13 b-\tfrac13 a=\tfrac23 a+\tfrac13 b.$

Chapter 11-Vectors.question_text: With the same triangle as in 3a, show that $AN:NB=1:2$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.hint: Use the similarity ratio from part (a) to relate $AN$ and $AB$, then deduce $NB$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.solution_text: From the similarity in part (a), $AN=\tfrac13 AB$ so the remaining segment is $NB=AB-AN=AB-\tfrac13 AB=\tfrac23 AB.$ Therefore $AN:NB=\tfrac13 AB:\tfrac23 AB=1:2.$

Chapter 11-Vectors.question_text: $OABC$ is a square. $M$ is the midpoint of $OA$, and $Q$ divides $BC$ in the ratio $1:3$. $AC$ and $MQ$ meet at $P$. If $\overrightarrow{OA}=a$ and $\overrightarrow{OC}=c$, express $\overrightarrow{OP}$ in terms of $a$ and $c$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.hint: Express all relevant points in terms of $a$ and $c$, form vector equations for lines $AC$ and $MQ$, then solve for the intersection parameter.
Chapter 11-Vectors.solution_text: In the square, $A$ has position $a$, $C$ has $c$ and $B$ has $a+c$. Midpoint $M$ of $OA$ has $\overrightarrow{OM}=\tfrac12a$. Point $Q$ divides $BC$ in the ratio $1:3$ with $BQ:QC=1:3$, so $\overrightarrow{OQ}=\tfrac34\overrightarrow{OB}+\tfrac14\overrightarrow{OC}=\tfrac34(a+c)+\tfrac14c=\tfrac34a+c$. Then $\overrightarrow{MQ}=\overrightarrow{OQ}-\overrightarrow{OM}=(\tfrac34a+c)-\tfrac12a=\tfrac14a+c$. A general point on $AC$ is $a+t(c-a)=(1-t)a+tc$, while a general point on $MQ$ is $\tfrac12a+s(\tfrac14a+c)=(\tfrac12+\tfrac{s}{4})a+sc$. At $P$ these are equal, so $(1-t)a+tc=(\tfrac12+\tfrac{s}{4})a+sc$, giving $1-t=\tfrac12+\tfrac{s}{4}$ and $t=s$. Hence $1-t=\tfrac12+\tfrac{t}{4}\Rightarrow4-4t=2+t\Rightarrow2=5t\Rightarrow t=\tfrac25$. Thus $\overrightarrow{OP}=\overrightarrow{OA}+t(\overrightarrow{OC}-\overrightarrow{OA})=a+\tfrac25(c-a)=\tfrac35a+\tfrac25c$.

Chapter 11-Vectors.question_text: Show that $P$ divides $AC$ in the ratio $2:3$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.hint: Use the parameter $t$ found on line $AC$ as the fraction of $AC$ from $A$ to $P$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.solution_text: From part (a), the position of $P$ on $AC$ is $a+t(c-a)$ with $t=\tfrac25$. This means $AP=\tfrac25\,AC$ and therefore $PC=AC-AP=\tfrac35\,AC$. Hence $AP:PC=2:3$, so $P$ divides $AC$ in the ratio $2:3$.

Chapter 11-Vectors.question_text: In triangle $ABC$ the position vectors of $A,B$ and $C$ are $\begin{pmatrix}5\\8\end{pmatrix}$, $\begin{pmatrix}4\\3\end{pmatrix}$ and $\begin{pmatrix}7\\6\end{pmatrix}$ respectively. Find $|\overrightarrow{AB}|$.
Using the same triangle, find $|\overrightarrow{AC}|$.
Using the same triangle, find $|\overrightarrow{BC}|$.
Find the sizes of $\angle BAC$, $\angle ABC$ and $\angle ACB$ to the nearest degree.
Chapter 11-Vectors.hint: Use the dot-product formula $\cos\theta=\dfrac{\vec{u}\cdot\vec{v}}{|\vec{u}||\vec{v}|}$ for the angle between two vectors from the same vertex.
Chapter 11-Vectors.solution_text: At $A$, use $\overrightarrow{AB}=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\-5\end{pmatrix}$ and $\overrightarrow{AC}=\begin{pmatrix}2\\-2\end{pmatrix}$: $\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot\overrightarrow{AC}=(-1)(2)+(-5)(-2)=-2+10=8$, $|\overrightarrow{AB}||\overrightarrow{AC}|=\sqrt{26}\cdot2\sqrt2=4\sqrt{13}$, so $\cos\angle BAC=\dfrac{8}{4\sqrt{13}}=\dfrac{2}{\sqrt{13}}\approx0.555$ giving $\angle BAC\approx56^\circ$. At $B$, use $\overrightarrow{BA}=-\overrightarrow{AB}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\5\end{pmatrix}$ and $\overrightarrow{BC}=\begin{pmatrix}3\\3\end{pmatrix}$: $\overrightarrow{BA}\cdot\overrightarrow{BC}=1\cdot3+5\cdot3=18$, $|\overrightarrow{BA}||\overrightarrow{BC}|=\sqrt{26}\cdot3\sqrt2=6\sqrt{13}$, so $\cos\angle ABC=\dfrac{18}{6\sqrt{13}}=\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{13}}\approx0.832$ giving $\angle ABC\approx34^\circ$. At $C$, use $\overrightarrow{CA}=-\overrightarrow{AC}=\begin{pmatrix}-2\\2\end{pmatrix}$ and $\overrightarrow{CB}=-\overrightarrow{BC}=\begin{pmatrix}-3\\-3\end{pmatrix}$: $\overrightarrow{CA}\cdot\overrightarrow{CB}=(-2)(-3)+2(-3)=6-6=0$, hence $\cos\angle ACB=0$ and $\angle ACB=90^\circ$. So the angles are approximately $56^\circ$, $34^\circ$ and $90^\circ$.

Chapter 11-Vectors.question_text: $\triangle OPQ$ is a triangle with $2\overrightarrow{PR}=\overrightarrow{RQ}$ and $3\overrightarrow{OR}=\overrightarrow{OS}$. Given $\overrightarrow{OP}=a$ and $\overrightarrow{OQ}=b$, show that $\overrightarrow{OS}=2a+b$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.hint: Use the section formula for point $R$ on $PQ$, then multiply $\overrightarrow{OR}$ by $3$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.solution_text: The condition $2\overrightarrow{PR}=\overrightarrow{RQ}$ gives $PR:RQ=1:2$, so $R$ divides $PQ$ in the ratio $1:2$. Thus $\overrightarrow{OR}=\dfrac{2\overrightarrow{OP}+1\overrightarrow{OQ}}{1+2}=\dfrac{2a+b}{3}$. Since $3\overrightarrow{OR}=\overrightarrow{OS}$, we get $\overrightarrow{OS}=3\cdot\dfrac{2a+b}{3}=2a+b$.

Chapter 11-Vectors.question_text: Point $T$ is added so that $\overrightarrow{OT}=-b$. Prove that points $T,P,S$ lie on a straight line.
Chapter 11-Vectors.hint: Show that $\overrightarrow{TP}$ and $\overrightarrow{TS}$ are parallel by expressing them in terms of $a$ and $b$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.solution_text: From $\overrightarrow{OP}=a$, $\overrightarrow{OS}=2a+b$ and $\overrightarrow{OT}=-b$, we have $\overrightarrow{TP}=\overrightarrow{OP}-\overrightarrow{OT}=a-(-b)=a+b$ and $\overrightarrow{TS}=\overrightarrow{OS}-\overrightarrow{OT}=(2a+b)-(-b)=2a+2b=2(a+b)$. Since $\overrightarrow{TS}=2\overrightarrow{TP}$, the vectors $\overrightarrow{TP}$ and $\overrightarrow{TS}$ are parallel and share point $T$, so $T,P,S$ lie on a straight line.

Chapter 11-Vectors.question_text: $OPQR$ is a parallelogram, with $\overrightarrow{OP}=a$ and $\overrightarrow{OR}=b$. $N$ is the midpoint of $PQ$ and $M$ is the midpoint of $QR$. The line $ON$ meets the diagonal $PR$ at $X$. Explain why $\overrightarrow{PX}=-ja+jb$, where $j$ is a constant.
Chapter 11-Vectors.hint: Parametrise the diagonal $PR$ from $P$ towards $R$ and write $\overrightarrow{PX}$ as a scalar multiple of $\overrightarrow{PR}$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.solution_text: On the diagonal $PR$, any point $X$ can be written as $X=P+j\,\overrightarrow{PR}$ for some real constant $j$, so $\overrightarrow{PX}=j\,\overrightarrow{PR}=j(b-a)=-ja+jb$, hence $\overrightarrow{PX}=-ja+jb$ for some constant $j$.

Chapter 11-Vectors.question_text: Show that $\overrightarrow{PX}=(k-1)a+\tfrac12kb$, where $k$ is a constant, given that $X$ also lies on the line $ON$ from the origin.
Chapter 11-Vectors.hint: Find $\overrightarrow{ON}$ using the midpoint $N$ of $PQ$, then write $\overrightarrow{OX}=k\,\overrightarrow{ON}$ and subtract $\overrightarrow{OP}$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.solution_text: In the parallelogram, $P$ has position $a$ and $Q$ has position $a+b$, so their midpoint $N$ has $\overrightarrow{ON}=\dfrac{\overrightarrow{OP}+\overrightarrow{OQ}}{2}=\dfrac{a+(a+b)}{2}=a+\tfrac12 b$. Any point $X$ on $ON$ has $\overrightarrow{OX}=k(a+\tfrac12 b)$, so $\overrightarrow{PX}=\overrightarrow{OX}-\overrightarrow{OP}=k(a+\tfrac12 b)-a=(k-1)a+\tfrac12kb$.

Chapter 11-Vectors.question_text: Explain why the constants $j$ and $k$ must satisfy the simultaneous equations $k-1=-j$ and $\tfrac12k=j$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.hint: Equate the two expressions for $\overrightarrow{PX}$ obtained in parts (a) and (b) and compare coefficients of $a$ and $b$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.solution_text: From part (a), $\overrightarrow{PX}=-ja+jb$ and from part (b), $\overrightarrow{PX}=(k-1)a+\tfrac12kb$. Since these are equal vectors, their $a$-components and $b$-components must match: $(k-1)a=-ja$ gives $k-1=-j$, and $\tfrac12kb=jb$ gives $\tfrac12k=j$. Thus $k-1=-j$ and $\tfrac12k=j$.

Chapter 11-Vectors.question_text: Hence find the values of $j$ and $k$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.solution_text: From $\tfrac12k=j$ substitute into $k-1=-j$ to get $k-1=-\tfrac12k$, so $k+\tfrac12k=1$ gives $\tfrac32k=1$ and therefore $k=\dfrac{2}{3}$. Then $j=\tfrac12k=\tfrac12\cdot\dfrac{2}{3}=\dfrac{1}{3}$. So $k=\dfrac23$ and $j=\dfrac13$.

Chapter 11-Vectors.question_title: Division of diagonal $PR$ into three equal parts
Chapter 11-Vectors.question_text: Deduce that the lines $ON$ and $OM$ divide the diagonal $PR$ into three equal parts.
Chapter 11-Vectors.hint: Use $j=\tfrac13$ to locate $X$ on $PR$ and similarly find the parameter for $Y$ where $OM$ meets $PR$, then compare the segments along $PR$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.solution_text: From part (a), $\overrightarrow{PX}=j\,\overrightarrow{PR}$ and with $j=\tfrac13$ we have $\overrightarrow{PX}=\tfrac13\overrightarrow{PR}$ so $X$ is one third of the way from $P$ to $R$. For the line $OM$, note that $M$ is the midpoint of $QR$ so $Q$ has position $a+b$ and $R$ has $b$, giving $\overrightarrow{OM}=\dfrac{(a+b)+b}{2}=\tfrac12a+b$. A general point $Y$ on $OM$ has $\overrightarrow{OY}=\lambda(\tfrac12a+b)$, and as a point on $PR$ also $\overrightarrow{OY}=\overrightarrow{OP}+t\,\overrightarrow{PR}=a+t(b-a)$ for some $t$. Equating components: from $b$ we get $\lambda=t$, and from $a$ we get $\tfrac12\lambda=1-t$. Substituting $\lambda=t$ gives $\tfrac12t=1-t$ so $\tfrac32t=1$ and $t=\dfrac{2}{3}$. Thus $\overrightarrow{PY}=t\,\overrightarrow{PR}=\dfrac23\overrightarrow{PR}$ so $Y$ is two thirds of the way from $P$ to $R$. Hence $PX=\tfrac13PR$, $PY=\tfrac23PR$, so $XY=PY-PX=\tfrac23PR-\tfrac13PR=\tfrac13PR$ and $YR=PR-PY=\tfrac13PR$. Therefore $PX=XY=YR$ and the lines $ON$ and $OM$ divide the diagonal $PR$ into three equal parts.

Chapter 11-Vectors.question_text: A particle $P$ is accelerating at a constant rate. When $t=0$, $P$ has velocity $\mathbf{u}=(2\mathbf{i}+3\mathbf{j})\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ and at time $t=5\ \text{s}$, $P$ has velocity $\mathbf{v}=(16\mathbf{i}-5\mathbf{j})\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. The acceleration vector is given by $\mathbf{a}=\dfrac{\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{u}}{t}$. Find the acceleration of $P$ in terms of $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.hint: Subtract the initial velocity from the final velocity, then divide by the time interval $5$ s.

Chapter 11-Vectors.question_text: A particle $P$ of mass $m=0.3\ \text{kg}$ moves under a single constant force $\mathbf{F}$ newtons. The acceleration of $P$ is $\mathbf{a}=(5\mathbf{i}+7\mathbf{j})\ \text{m s}^{-2}$. Find the angle between the acceleration and $\mathbf{i}$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.hint: UUse $\tan\theta = \dfrac{\text{y-component}}{\text{x-component}} = \dfrac{7}{5}$ for the angle to the positive $x$-axis.

Chapter 11-Vectors.question_text: With the information in 5a and using $\mathbf{F}=m\mathbf{a}$, find the magnitude of $\mathbf{F}$.

Two forces $\mathbf{F}_1$ and $\mathbf{F}_2$ are given by $\mathbf{F}_1=(3\mathbf{i}-4\mathbf{j})\ \text{N}$ and $\mathbf{F}_2=(p\mathbf{i}+q\mathbf{j})\ \text{N}$. The resultant force $\mathbf{R}=\mathbf{F}_1+\mathbf{F}_2$ acts in a direction parallel to the vector $(2\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j})$. Find the angle between $\mathbf{R}$ and the vector $\mathbf{i}$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.hint: Since $\mathbf{R}$ is parallel to $2\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}$, use the angle between $2\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}$ and $\mathbf{i}$: $\cos\theta=\dfrac{\vec v\cdot\mathbf{i}}{|\vec v||\mathbf{i}|}$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.solution_text: Let $\vec v=2\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}=(2,-1)$. Then $\vec v\cdot\mathbf{i}=2$, $|\vec v|=\sqrt{2^{2}+(-1)^{2}}=\sqrt{5}$, $|\mathbf{i}|=1$. Hence $\cos\theta=\dfrac{2}{\sqrt5}$ so $\theta=\cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{2}{\sqrt5}\right)\approx26.6^\circ.$

Chapter 11-Vectors.question_text: Show that $p+2q=5$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.solution_text: $\mathbf{R}=(3+p)\mathbf{i}+(-4+q)\mathbf{j}$ is parallel to $2\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}$, so $\mathbf{R}=k(2\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j})=(2k)\mathbf{i}+(-k)\mathbf{j}$. Thus $3+p=2k$ and $-4+q=-k$, so $k=4-q$. Substituting $k$ into $3+p=2(4-q)$ gives $3+p=8-2q\Rightarrow p+2q=5.$

Chapter 11-Vectors.question_text: Given that $p=1$, find the magnitude of $\mathbf{R}$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.hint: First find $q$ from $p+2q=5$, then compute $\mathbf{R}=\mathbf{F}_1+\mathbf{F}_2$ and its magnitude.
Chapter 11-Vectors.solution_text: From $p+2q=5$ with $p=1$ we get $1+2q=5\Rightarrow2q=4\Rightarrow q=2$. Then $\mathbf{F}_2=\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{j}$ and $\mathbf{R}=(3\mathbf{i}-4\mathbf{j})+(\mathbf{i}+2\mathbf{j})=(4\mathbf{i}-2\mathbf{j})$. Hence $|\mathbf{R}|=\sqrt{4^{2}+(-2)^{2}}=\sqrt{16+4}=\sqrt{20}=2\sqrt5\ \text{N}.$

Chapter 11-Vectors.question_text: The field $ABC$ is a triangle. Given $\overrightarrow{AB}=30\mathbf{i}+40\mathbf{j}$ metres and $\overrightarrow{AC}=40\mathbf{i}-60\mathbf{j}$ metres, find $\overrightarrow{BC}$.
Find the size of $\angle BAC$, in degrees, correct to one decimal place.
Find the area of the field in square metres.
Chapter 11-Vectors.hint: Use the $2$-D vector cross-product magnitude: $\text{Area}=\dfrac12|\overrightarrow{AB}\times\overrightarrow{AC}|$, where $|\vec u\times\vec v|=|u_xv_y-u_yv_x|$.

Chapter 11-Vectors.question_text: A boat has position vector $(2\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j})$ km and a buoy has position vector $(6\mathbf{i}-4\mathbf{j})$ km relative to origin $O$. Find the distance of the boat from the buoy.
Chapter 11-Vectors.hint: Form the displacement vector from boat to buoy and find its magnitude.

Chapter 11-Vectors.question_text: Find the bearing of the boat from the buoy.
Chapter 11-Vectors.hint: Use the vector from buoy to boat $(-4\mathbf{i}+5\mathbf{j})$; find angle from north using $\tan\theta=\dfrac{\text{east}}{\text{north}}$ and convert to a bearing $0^\circ$–$360^\circ$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.solution_text: Vector from buoy to boat is $(2\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j})-(6\mathbf{i}-4\mathbf{j})=(-4\mathbf{i}+5\mathbf{j})$, i.e. $4$ km west and $5$ km north. Let $\theta$ be the angle west of north: $\tan\theta=\dfrac{4}{5}\Rightarrow\theta\approx38.7^\circ.$ Bearings are measured clockwise from north; going towards the northwest gives bearing $360^\circ-\theta\approx360^\circ-38.7^\circ\approx321^\circ.$

Chapter 11-Vectors.question_text: The boat travels with constant velocity $(8\mathbf{i}-10\mathbf{j})$ km h$^{-1}$. Verify that the boat is travelling directly towards the buoy and find the speed of the boat.
Chapter 11-Vectors.hint: Compare the direction of the velocity with the displacement from boat to buoy; if they are scalar multiples the motion is directly towards the buoy. Speed is the magnitude of velocity.
Chapter 11-Vectors.solution_text: The displacement from boat to buoy is $(4\mathbf{i}-5\mathbf{j})$. The velocity $\mathbf{v}=(8\mathbf{i}-10\mathbf{j})=2(4\mathbf{i}-5\mathbf{j})$ is a positive scalar multiple of this displacement, so the boat travels directly towards the buoy. The speed is $|\mathbf{v}|=\sqrt{8^{2}+(-10)^{2}}=\sqrt{64+100}=\sqrt{164}=2\sqrt{41}\ \text{km h}^{-1}.$

Chapter 11-Vectors.question_text: Work out how long it will take the boat to reach the buoy.

Two forces $\mathbf{F}_1$ and $\mathbf{F}_2$ act on a particle. $\mathbf{F}_1=-3\mathbf{i}+7\mathbf{j}$ newtons and $\mathbf{F}_2=\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}$ newtons. The resultant force $\mathbf{R}$ is given by $\mathbf{R}=\mathbf{F}_1+\mathbf{F}_2$. Calculate the magnitude of $\mathbf{R}$ in newtons.
Chapter 11-Vectors.hint: Add the two vectors to get $\mathbf{R}$, then find its magnitude $|\mathbf{R}|=\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}}$.

Chapter 11-Vectors.question_text: With $\mathbf{R}=-2\mathbf{i}+6\mathbf{j}$ from part (a), calculate, to the nearest degree, the angle between the line of action of $\mathbf{R}$ and the vector $\mathbf{j}$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.hint: Use the dot product formula $\cos\theta=\dfrac{\mathbf{R}\cdot\mathbf{j}}{|\mathbf{R}||\mathbf{j}|}$, where $\mathbf{j}=(0,1)$.

Chapter 11-Vectors.question_text: At $09{:}00$, a small boat $S$ has position vector $(-2\mathbf{i}-4\mathbf{j})$ km relative to a fixed origin $O$ (with $\mathbf{i}$ due east and $\mathbf{j}$ due north). At $09{:}40$, $S$ is at $(4\mathbf{i}-6\mathbf{j})$ km. Calculate the bearing on which $S$ is drifting.
Chapter 11-Vectors.hint: Find the displacement vector $\overrightarrow{OS_2}-\overrightarrow{OS_1}$, resolve into east and north components, then convert its direction into a three-figure bearing measured clockwise from north.
Chapter 11-Vectors.solution_text: Initial position $\overrightarrow{OS_1}=(-2,-4)$, final position $\overrightarrow{OS_2}=(4,-6)$. Displacement $\overrightarrow{S_1S_2}=\overrightarrow{OS_2}-\overrightarrow{OS_1}=(4,-6)-(-2,-4)=(6,-2)$, i.e.\ $6$ km east and $2$ km south. The direction is $E\,\theta\,S$ where $\tan\theta=\dfrac{2}{6}=\dfrac{1}{3}$, so $\theta=\tan^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)\approx18.4^\circ$. Bearing from north is $090^\circ+\theta\approx90^\circ+18.4^\circ=108.4^\circ\approx108^\circ$ (to nearest degree).

Chapter 11-Vectors.question_text: With the same information, find the speed of $S$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.hint: Speed $=\dfrac{\text{distance travelled}}{\text{time}}$; use the magnitude of the displacement and time $40$ minutes $=\dfrac{2}{3}$ h.

Chapter 11-Vectors.question_text: A football is kicked from point $A$ and its motion is modelled as a particle with constant velocity $(4\mathbf{i}+9\mathbf{j})\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. Find the speed of the ball.
Chapter 11-Vectors.hint: Speed is the magnitude of the velocity vector: $|\vec v|=\sqrt{4^{2}+9^{2}}$.

Chapter 11-Vectors.question_text: Using the same model, find the distance of the ball from $A$ after $6$ seconds.
Chapter 11-Vectors.hint: Distance travelled with constant speed is $\text{speed}\times\text{time}$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.solution_text: From part (a) the speed is $\sqrt{97}\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. In $6$ s, distance $=\sqrt{97}\times6=6\sqrt{97}\ \text{m}.$

Chapter 11-Vectors.question_text: Comment on the validity of this constant-velocity model for large values of $t$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.hint: Consider real motion of a ball under gravity and air resistance compared with a constant-velocity assumption.
Chapter 11-Vectors.solution_text: In reality the ball is subject to gravity and air resistance, so its velocity changes: it follows a curved trajectory, slows down, and eventually lands, bounces or stops. The assumption of constant velocity is only reasonable for a very short time immediately after the kick; for large $t$ the model is not valid because it ignores these forces and the ball cannot continue indefinitely in a straight line at constant speed.

Chapter 11-Vectors.question_text: $ABCD$ is a trapezium with $AB\parallel DC$ and $DC=4AB$. Point $M$ divides $DC$ such that $DM:MC=3:2$. Given $\overrightarrow{AB}=a$ and $\overrightarrow{BC}=b$, find $\overrightarrow{AM}$ in terms of $a$ and $b$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.hint: Take $A$ as origin, find position vectors of $B,C,D,M$, then subtract to obtain $\overrightarrow{AM}$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.solution_text: Let $A$ be the origin. Then $\overrightarrow{AB}=a\Rightarrow B:a$, $\overrightarrow{BC}=b\Rightarrow C:a+b$. Since $DC=4AB$, $\overrightarrow{DC}=4a$ so $C=D+4a\Rightarrow D=(a+b)-4a=-3a+b$. With $DM:MC=3:2$, $\overrightarrow{DM}=\dfrac{3}{5}\overrightarrow{DC}=\dfrac{3}{5}\cdot4a=\dfrac{12}{5}a$, so $M=D+\overrightarrow{DM}=(-3a+b)+\dfrac{12}{5}a=-\dfrac{3}{5}a+b$. Thus $\overrightarrow{AM}=\overrightarrow{OM}=-\dfrac{3}{5}a+b$.

Chapter 11-Vectors.question_text: In the same trapezium, find $\overrightarrow{BD}$ in terms of $a$ and $b$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.hint: Use the position vectors $B:a$ and $D=-3a+b$ and subtract.

Chapter 11-Vectors.question_text: In the same trapezium, find $\overrightarrow{MB}$ in terms of $a$ and $b$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.hint: Subtract the position vector of $M$ from that of $B$.

Chapter 11-Vectors.question_text: In the same trapezium, find $\overrightarrow{DA}$ in terms of $a$ and $b$.
The vectors $5a+kb$ and $8a+2b$ are parallel. Find the value of $k$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.hint: If $5a+kb$ is parallel to $8a+2b$ then $5a+kb=\lambda(8a+2b)$ for some $\lambda$; equate coefficients of $a$ and $b$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.solution_text: Assume $5a+kb=\lambda(8a+2b)=8\lambda a+2\lambda b$. Then $5=8\lambda$ and $k=2\lambda$. From $5=8\lambda$ we get $\lambda=\dfrac{5}{8}$, hence $k=2\lambda=2\cdot\dfrac{5}{8}=\dfrac{5}{4}$.

Chapter 11-Vectors.question_text: Given $a=\begin{pmatrix}7\\4\end{pmatrix}$, $b=\begin{pmatrix}10\\-2\end{pmatrix}$ and $c=\begin{pmatrix}-5\\-3\end{pmatrix}$, find $a+b+c$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.hint: Add the components of the three vectors.

Chapter 11-Vectors.question_text: With the same $a,b,c$, find $2a-2b+c$.
With the same $a,b,c$, find $2a+2b-3c$.
In triangle $ABC$, $\overrightarrow{AB}=3\mathbf{i}+5\mathbf{j}$ and $\overrightarrow{AC}=6\mathbf{i}+3\mathbf{j}$. Find $\overrightarrow{BC}$.
In the same triangle, find $\angle BAC$ to one decimal place.
Chapter 11-Vectors.solution_text: Let $\overrightarrow{AB}=(3,5)$ and $\overrightarrow{AC}=(6,3)$. Then $\overrightarrow{AB}\cdot\overrightarrow{AC}=3\cdot6+5\cdot3=18+15=33$. Also $|\overrightarrow{AB}|=\sqrt{3^{2}+5^{2}}=\sqrt{34}$, $|\overrightarrow{AC}|=\sqrt{6^{2}+3^{2}}=\sqrt{45}=3\sqrt{5}$. Hence $\cos\angle BAC=\dfrac{33}{\sqrt{34}\cdot3\sqrt{5}}=\dfrac{11}{\sqrt{170}}\approx0.8437$, so $\angle BAC\approx\cos^{-1}(0.8437)\approx32.2^\circ$ (to $1$ d.p.).

Chapter 11-Vectors.question_text: Using $\overrightarrow{AB}$ and $\overrightarrow{AC}$, find the area of $\triangle ABC$.
The resultant of vectors $a=4\mathbf{i}-3\mathbf{j}$ and $b=2p\,\mathbf{i}-p\,\mathbf{j}$ is parallel to $c=2\mathbf{i}-3\mathbf{j}$. Find the value of $p$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.hint: Set $\mathbf{R}=a+b$ and require $\mathbf{R}=\lambda c$ for some $\lambda$; compare components to solve for $p$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.solution_text: $\mathbf{R}=a+b=(4+2p)\mathbf{i}+(-3-p)\mathbf{j}$. If $\mathbf{R}$ is parallel to $c=2\mathbf{i}-3\mathbf{j}$ then $(4+2p,-3-p)=\lambda(2,-3)=(2\lambda,-3\lambda)$. Hence $4+2p=2\lambda$ and $-3-p=-3\lambda$. From the second: $3\lambda=3+p\Rightarrow\lambda=1+\dfrac{p}{3}$. Substitute into the first: $4+2p=2\left(1+\dfrac{p}{3}\right)=2+\dfrac{2p}{3}\Rightarrow2=\dfrac{2p}{3}-2p=-\dfrac{4p}{3}\Rightarrow p=-\dfrac{3}{2}$.

Chapter 11-Vectors.question_text: For the value of $p$ found in 8a, find the resultant of $a$ and $b$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.hint: Substitute $p=-\dfrac{3}{2}$ into $\mathbf{R}=a+b$ or use $\mathbf{R}=\lambda c$ with $\lambda$ from the working.
Chapter 11-Vectors.solution_text: With $p=-\dfrac{3}{2}$, $b=2p\,\mathbf{i}-p\,\mathbf{j}=-3\mathbf{i}+\dfrac{3}{2}\mathbf{j}$, so $\mathbf{R}=a+b=(4-3)\mathbf{i}+(-3+\dfrac{3}{2})\mathbf{j}=\mathbf{i}-\dfrac{3}{2}\mathbf{j}$. (Equivalently, from the equations we get $\lambda=\dfrac12$ and $\mathbf{R}=\dfrac12(2\mathbf{i}-3\mathbf{j})=\mathbf{i}-\dfrac{3}{2}\mathbf{j}$.)

Chapter 11-Vectors.question_text: For vector $a=8\mathbf{i}+15\mathbf{j}$, (i) find a unit vector in the same direction, (ii) find the angle the vector makes with $\mathbf{i}$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.hint: Use $\hat{a}=\dfrac{\vec a}{|\vec a|}$ and $\cos\theta=\dfrac{\vec a\cdot\mathbf{i}}{|\vec a||\mathbf{i}|}=\dfrac{\text{$x$-component}}{|\vec a|}$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.solution_text: $|\vec a|=\sqrt{8^{2}+15^{2}}=\sqrt{64+225}=\sqrt{289}=17$, so the unit vector is $\hat{a}=\dfrac{1}{17}(8\mathbf{i}+15\mathbf{j})=\dfrac{8}{17}\mathbf{i}+\dfrac{15}{17}\mathbf{j}$. The angle with $\mathbf{i}$ satisfies $\cos\theta=\dfrac{8}{17}$, so $\theta=\cos^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{8}{17}\right)\approx62.0^\circ$.

Chapter 11-Vectors.question_text: For vector $b=24\mathbf{i}-7\mathbf{j}$, (i) find a unit vector in the same direction, (ii) find the angle the vector makes with $\mathbf{i}$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.hint: Find $|\vec b|$, divide to get the unit vector, then use $\cos\theta=\dfrac{24}{|\vec b|}$.

Chapter 11-Vectors.question_text: For vector $c=-9\mathbf{i}+40\mathbf{j}$, (i) find a unit vector in the same direction, (ii) find the angle the vector makes with $\mathbf{i}$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.hint: Compute magnitude $|\vec c|$, then $\hat{c}=\vec c/|\vec c|$ and $\cos\theta=\dfrac{-9}{|\vec c|}$.

Chapter 11-Vectors.question_text: For vector $d=3\mathbf{i}-2\mathbf{j}$, (i) find a unit vector in the same direction, (ii) find the angle the vector makes with $\mathbf{i}$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.hint: Find $|\vec d|$, then $\hat{d}=\vec d/|\vec d|$ and $\cos\theta=\dfrac{3}{|\vec d|}$.

Chapter 11-Vectors.question_text: The vector $\mathbf{a}=p\mathbf{i}+q\mathbf{j}$, where $p$ and $q$ are positive constants, is such that $\lvert\mathbf{a}\rvert=15$. Given that $\mathbf{a}$ makes an angle of $55^\circ$ with $\mathbf{i}$, find the values of $p$ and $q$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.solution_text: $|\mathbf{a}|=\sqrt{p^{2}+q^{2}}=15\Rightarrow p^{2}+q^{2}=225$. Since $\mathbf{a}$ makes angle $55^\circ$ with $\mathbf{i}$, its components are $p=15\cos55^\circ$ and $q=15\sin55^\circ$. Thus $p=15\cos55^\circ,\ q=15\sin55^\circ$ (both positive).

Chapter 11-Vectors.question_text: Given that $\lvert 3\mathbf{i}-k\mathbf{j}\rvert=3\sqrt{5}$, find the value of $k$.

In $\triangle OAB$, $\overrightarrow{OA}=\mathbf{a}$ and $\overrightarrow{OB}=\mathbf{b}$. The point $M$ divides $OA$ in the ratio $3:2$ and $MN$ is parallel to $OB$. Express the vector $\overrightarrow{ON}$ in terms of $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.hint: Write $\overrightarrow{OM}$ as a fraction of $\mathbf{a}$, then let $\overrightarrow{ON}= \mathbf{a}+t(\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a})$ (since $N$ lies on $AB$) and use $MN\parallel\mathbf{b}$ to find $t$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.solution_text: $OM:MA=3:2\Rightarrow\overrightarrow{OM}=\dfrac{3}{5}\mathbf{a}$. Let $N$ lie on $AB$, so $\overrightarrow{ON}=\mathbf{a}+t(\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a})=(1-t)\mathbf{a}+t\mathbf{b}$. Then $\overrightarrow{MN}=\overrightarrow{ON}-\overrightarrow{OM}=(1-t)\mathbf{a}+t\mathbf{b}-\dfrac{3}{5}\mathbf{a}=\left(\dfrac{2}{5}-t\right)\mathbf{a}+t\mathbf{b}$. For $\overrightarrow{MN}\parallel\mathbf{b}$, the coefficient of $\mathbf{a}$ must be $0$, so $\dfrac{2}{5}-t=0\Rightarrow t=\dfrac{2}{5}$. Hence $\overrightarrow{ON}=(1-\dfrac{2}{5})\mathbf{a}+\dfrac{2}{5}\mathbf{b}=\dfrac{3}{5}\mathbf{a}+\dfrac{2}{5}\mathbf{b}$.

Chapter 11-Vectors.question_text: With the information of Question 12, find the vector $\overrightarrow{MN}$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.hint: Use $\overrightarrow{MN}=\overrightarrow{ON}-\overrightarrow{OM}$ with the results from part (a).

Chapter 11-Vectors.question_text: Still in Question 12, show that $AN:NB=2:3$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.hint: Express $\overrightarrow{AN}$ and $\overrightarrow{NB}$ as multiples of $\mathbf{b}-\mathbf{a}$ and compare their magnitudes.

Chapter 11-Vectors.question_text: Two forces $\mathbf{F}_1=(4\mathbf{i}-5\mathbf{j})$ N and $\mathbf{F}_2=(p\mathbf{i}+q\mathbf{j})$ N act on a particle. The resultant $\mathbf{R}=\mathbf{F}_1+\mathbf{F}_2$ acts in a direction parallel to the vector $(3\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j})$. Find the angle between $\mathbf{R}$ and the vector $\mathbf{i}$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.hint: Since $\mathbf{R}\parallel(3\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j})$, the angle equals the angle between $(3\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j})$ and $\mathbf{i}$; use $\cos\theta=\dfrac{\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{i}}{|\mathbf{v}|}$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.solution_text: The direction vector is $\mathbf{v}=3\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j}$. Then $\mathbf{v}\cdot\mathbf{i}=3$, $|\mathbf{v}|=\sqrt{3^{2}+(-1)^{2}}=\sqrt{10}$. Hence $\cos\theta=\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{10}}$ and $\theta=\cos^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{3}{\sqrt{10}}\right)$ (approximately $18.4^\circ$).

Chapter 11-Vectors.question_text: With the same information, show that $p+3q=11$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.hint: Let $\mathbf{R}=(4+p)\mathbf{i}+(-5+q)\mathbf{j}$ and set $\mathbf{R}=\lambda(3\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j})$; compare coefficients of $\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{j}$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.solution_text: $\mathbf{R}=\mathbf{F}_1+\mathbf{F}_2=(4+p)\mathbf{i}+(-5+q)\mathbf{j}$. Since $\mathbf{R}=\lambda(3\mathbf{i}-\mathbf{j})=(3\lambda)\mathbf{i}+(-\lambda)\mathbf{j}$, we have $4+p=3\lambda$ and $-5+q=-\lambda\Rightarrow\lambda=5-q$. Substituting gives $4+p=3(5-q)=15-3q\Rightarrow p+3q=11$.

Chapter 11-Vectors.question_text: Given that $p=2$, find the magnitude of $\mathbf{R}$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.hint: Use $p+3q=11$ to find $q$, then compute $\mathbf{R}$ and its magnitude.
Chapter 11-Vectors.solution_text: From $p+3q=11$ with $p=2$ we get $2+3q=11\Rightarrow3q=9\Rightarrow q=3$. Then $\mathbf{R}=(4+p)\mathbf{i}+(-5+q)\mathbf{j}=(4+2)\mathbf{i}+(-5+3)\mathbf{j}=6\mathbf{i}-2\mathbf{j}$. Its magnitude is $|\mathbf{R}|=\sqrt{6^{2}+(-2)^{2}}=\sqrt{36+4}=\sqrt{40}=2\sqrt{10}\ \text{N}$.

Chapter 11-Vectors.question_text: A particle $P$ accelerates at a constant rate. When $t=0$, $P$ has velocity $\mathbf{u}=(3\mathbf{i}+4\mathbf{j})\ \text{m s}^{-1}$ and at time $t=2\ \text{s}$, $P$ has velocity $\mathbf{v}=(15\mathbf{i}-3\mathbf{j})\ \text{m s}^{-1}$. The acceleration vector is given by $\mathbf{a}=\dfrac{\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{u}}{t}$. Find the magnitude of the acceleration of $P$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.hint: First compute $\mathbf{v}-\mathbf{u}$, divide by $t$ to get $\mathbf{a}$, then find $|\mathbf{a}|=\sqrt{x^{2}+y^{2}}$.

Chapter 11-Vectors.question_text: The point $B$ lies on the line with equation $3y=12-5x$. Given that $\lvert OB\rvert=\dfrac{3\sqrt{10}}{2}$, find two possible expressions for $\overrightarrow{OB}$ in the form $p\mathbf{i}+q\mathbf{j}$.
Chapter 11-Vectors.hint: Let $B=(x,y)$ satisfy both the line $3y=12-5x$ and the circle $x^{2}+y^{2}=\left(\dfrac{3\sqrt{10}}{2}\right)^{2}$; solve the simultaneous equations, then write the two corresponding vectors.
Chapter 11-Vectors.solution_text: Let $B=(x,y)$ with $3y=12-5x\Rightarrow y=\dfrac{12-5x}{3}$. The magnitude condition gives $x^{2}+y^{2}=x^{2}+\left(\dfrac{12-5x}{3}\right)^{2}=\left(\dfrac{3\sqrt{10}}{2}\right)^{2}=\dfrac{45}{2}$. Thus $x^{2}+\dfrac{(12-5x)^{2}}{9}=\dfrac{45}{2}$. Multiply by $18$: $18x^{2}+2(12-5x)^{2}=405\Rightarrow18x^{2}+2(144-120x+25x^{2})=405\Rightarrow68x^{2}-240x-117=0$. Solving gives $x=\dfrac{240\pm36\sqrt{69}}{136}=\dfrac{60\pm9\sqrt{69}}{34}$. Then $y=\dfrac{12-5x}{3}=\dfrac{36\mp15\sqrt{69}}{34}$. Hence the two possible position vectors are $\overrightarrow{OB}=\dfrac{60+9\sqrt{69}}{34}\,\mathbf{i}+\dfrac{36-15\sqrt{69}}{34}\,\mathbf{j}$ and $\overrightarrow{OB}=\dfrac{60-9\sqrt{69}}{34}\,\mathbf{i}+\dfrac{36+15\sqrt{69}}{34}\,\mathbf{j}$.

Chapter 12-Differentiation.question_text: for the curve $y=x^{2}-2x$, complete the table of gradient estimates at $x=-1,0,1,2,3$.
Chapter 12-Differentiation.hint: Use the derivative: $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=2x-2$, which gives the gradient at any $x$.

Chapter 12-Differentiation.question_text: at the point where $x=p$, write a hypothesis about the gradient of the curve.
estimate the gradient at the point $(1.5,-0.75)$ to test the hypothesis.
Chapter 12-Differentiation.solution_text: $\text{Predicted gradient}=2(1.5)-2=1.\ \text{A tangent estimate at }(1.5,-0.75)\text{ also gives }\approx1,\ \text{confirming the hypothesis.}$

Chapter 12-Differentiation.question_text: The diagram shows the curve with equation $y=\sqrt{1-x^{2}}$. The point $A$ has coordinates $(0.6,0.8)$. Verify that point $A$ lies on the curve.
Chapter 12-Differentiation.hint: Substitute $x=0.6$ into $y=\sqrt{1-x^{2}}$ and check that the $y$-value is $0.8$.
Chapter 12-Differentiation.solution_text: $A(0.6,0.8)$ lies on $y=\sqrt{1-x^{2}}$ if $0.8=\sqrt{1-0.6^{2}}$. Compute $1-0.6^{2}=1-0.36=0.64$ and $\sqrt{0.64}=0.8$. Since the $y$-value from the curve equals $0.8$, point $A$ lies on the curve.

Chapter 12-Differentiation.question_text: Use a ruler to estimate the gradient of the curve at point $A$.
Chapter 12-Differentiation.hint: Use the derivative of $y=\sqrt{1-x^{2}}$, namely $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=-\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}$, and evaluate it at $x=0.6$ to get an approximate gradient.
Chapter 12-Differentiation.solution_text: For $y=\sqrt{1-x^{2}}$ we have $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=-\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{1-x^{2}}}$. At $x=0.6$ this gives $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=-\dfrac{0.6}{\sqrt{1-0.6^{2}}}=-\dfrac{0.6}{\sqrt{0.64}}=-\dfrac{0.6}{0.8}=-0.75$. So the gradient at $A$ is approximately $-0.75$, which a ruler on the graph should confirm.

Chapter 12-Differentiation.question_text: Find the gradient of the line segments: (i) $AD$, (ii) $AC$, (iii) $AB$. The points $B,C,D$ lie on the curve $y=\sqrt{1-x^{2}}$ with $x$-coordinates $0.7,0.8,0.9$ respectively and $A=(0.6,0.8)$.
Chapter 12-Differentiation.hint: First find the $y$-coordinates of $B,C,D$ using $y=\sqrt{1-x^{2}}$, then use $\text{gradient}=\dfrac{y_{2}-y_{1}}{x_{2}-x_{1}}$ for each chord.

Chapter 12-Differentiation.question_text: Comment on the relationship between your answers to parts b and c.
Chapter 12-Differentiation.hint: Compare the chord gradients from part (c) with the tangent gradient from part (b); note how they change as the point on the curve gets closer to $A$.
Chapter 12-Differentiation.solution_text: The gradient of the tangent at $A$ from part (b) is about $-0.75$. The chord gradients from part (c) are $m_{AD}\approx-1.21$, $m_{AC}=-1$, $m_{AB}\approx-0.86$. As the point on the curve moves from $D$ to $C$ to $B$ (getting closer to $A$), the gradient of the chord becomes less negative and gets closer to $-0.75$. This shows that the tangent gradient is the limiting value of the gradients of chords through $A$ as the second point approaches $A$.

Chapter 12-Differentiation.question_text: $F$ is the point with coordinates $(3,9)$ on the curve $y=x^{2}$.\\ a Find the gradient of the chord joining the point $F$ to the point with coordinates $(4,16)$.
a Find the gradient of the chord joining $F(3,9)$ to $(3.5,12.25)$.
a Find the gradient of the chord joining $F(3,9)$ to $(3.1,9.61)$.
a Find the gradient of the chord joining $F(3,9)$ to $(3.01,9.0601)$.
a Find the gradient of the chord joining $F(3,9)$ to $(3+h,(3+h)^{2})$.
Chapter 12-Differentiation.hint: Write the gradient as a difference quotient and simplify algebraically.

Chapter 12-Differentiation.question_text: b What do you deduce about the gradient of the tangent at the point $(3,9)$?
Chapter 12-Differentiation.hint: Use the limiting value of the chord gradient $6+h$ as $h\to0$.
Chapter 12-Differentiation.solution_text: $$\text{Chord gradient}=6+h\ \Rightarrow\ \lim_{h\to0}(6+h)=6,\ \text{so the gradient of the tangent at }(3,9)\text{ is }6.$$

Chapter 12-Differentiation.question_text: $G$ is the point with coordinates $(4,16)$ on the curve $y=x^{2}$.\\ a Find the gradient of the chord joining $G$ to $(5,25)$.
a Find the gradient of the chord joining $G(4,16)$ to $(4.5,20.25)$.
a Find the gradient of the chord joining $G(4,16)$ to $(4.1,16.81)$.
a Find the gradient of the chord joining $G(4,16)$ to $(4.01,16.0801)$.
Chapter 12-Differentiation.hint: Again use the chord gradient formula.

Chapter 12-Differentiation.question_text: a Find the gradient of the chord joining $G(4,16)$ to $(4+h,(4+h)^{2})$.
Chapter 12-Differentiation.hint: Write the gradient as a difference quotient and simplify.

Chapter 12-Differentiation.question_text: b What do you deduce about the gradient of the tangent at the point $(4,16)$?
Chapter 12-Differentiation.hint: Use the limiting value of $8+h$ as $h\to0$.
Chapter 12-Differentiation.solution_text: $$\text{Chord gradient}=8+h\ \Rightarrow\ \lim_{h\to0}(8+h)=8,\ \text{so the gradient of the tangent at }(4,16)\text{ is }8.$$

Chapter 12-Differentiation.question_text: For the function $f(x)=x^{2}$, use the definition of the derivative to show that $f'(2)=4$.
For the function $f(x)=x^{2}$, use the definition of the derivative to show that $f'(-3)=-6$.
Chapter 12-Differentiation.hint: Apply the same limit formula with $a=-3$.

Chapter 12-Differentiation.question_text: For the function $f(x)=x^{2}$, use the definition of the derivative to show that $f'(0)=0$.
For the function $f(x)=x^{2}$, use the definition of the derivative to show that $f'(50)=100$.
For $f(x)=x^{2}$, a Show that $f'(x)=\displaystyle\lim_{h\to0}(2x+h)$.
b Hence deduce that $f'(x)=2x$.
Chapter 12-Differentiation.hint: Let $h\to0$ in the expression from part (a).

Chapter 12-Differentiation.question_text: The point $A$ with coordinates $(-2,-8)$ lies on the curve with equation $y=x^{3}$. At point $A$ the curve has gradient $g$. a Show that $g=\displaystyle\lim_{h\to0}(12-6h+h^{2})$.
Chapter 12-Differentiation.hint: Write the gradient at $x=-2$ as $\displaystyle\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(-2+h)-f(-2)}{h}$ with $f(x)=x^{3}$ and expand $(-2+h)^{3}$.

Chapter 12-Differentiation.question_text: b Deduce the value of $g$.
Chapter 12-Differentiation.hint: Evaluate the limit in part (a) as $h\to0$.

Chapter 12-Differentiation.question_text: The point $A$ with coordinates $(-1,4)$ lies on the curve with equation $y=x^{3}-5x$. The point $B$ also lies on the curve and has $x$-coordinate $(-1+h)$. a Show that the gradient of the line segment $AB$ is given by $h^{2}-3h-2$.
Chapter 12-Differentiation.hint: Use gradient $=\dfrac{f(-1+h)-f(-1)}{h}$ with $f(x)=x^{3}-5x$, expand $(-1+h)^{3}$ and simplify.

Chapter 12-Differentiation.solution_text: $$\begin{aligned}y&=\sin x+\cos x\\y'&=\frac{\pi}{180}(\cos x-\sin x)\\y'=0&\Rightarrow \cos x=\sin x\Rightarrow \tan x=1\\x&=45^\circ,\ 225^\circ\\y(45^\circ)&=\frac{\sqrt2}{2}+\frac{\sqrt2}{2}=\sqrt2\\y(225^\circ)&=-\frac{\sqrt2}{2}-\frac{\sqrt2}{2}=-\sqrt2\\y''&=-\left(\frac{\pi}{180}\right)^2(\sin x+\cos x)\\y''(45^\circ)&=-\left(\frac{\pi}{180}\right)^2\sqrt2<0\Rightarrow \text{local maximum at }(45^\circ,\sqrt2)\\y''(225^\circ)&=-\left(\frac{\pi}{180}\right)^2(-\sqrt2)>0\Rightarrow \text{local minimum at }(225^\circ,-\sqrt2)\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 12-Differentiation.question_text: For $y=2\sin x-\sqrt3\cos x$ (degrees), find $x$ in $0^\circ\le x\le360^\circ$ where $y'=0$.
Chapter 12-Differentiation.hint: Differentiate (degrees) then solve $2\cos x+\sqrt3\sin x=0\Rightarrow\tan x=-\frac{2}{\sqrt3}$.
Chapter 12-Differentiation.solution_text: $$\begin{aligned}y&=2\sin x-\sqrt3\cos x\\y'&=\frac{\pi}{180}\big(2\cos x+\sqrt3\sin x\big)\\y'=0&\Rightarrow 2\cos x+\sqrt3\sin x=0\\\sqrt3\sin x&=-2\cos x\Rightarrow\tan x=-\frac{2}{\sqrt3}\\\beta&=\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{2}{\sqrt3}\right)\approx49.107^\circ\\\tan x<0&\Rightarrow x=180^\circ-\beta,\ 360^\circ-\beta\\x&\approx130.893^\circ,\ 310.893^\circ\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 12-Differentiation.question_text: For $y=\sin x+\sin2x$ (degrees), find all points of inflection for $0^\circ\le x\le360^\circ$.
Chapter 12-Differentiation.hint: Compute $y''$ carefully with degree factor $(\pi/180)^2$, solve $y''=0$ and check sign change.
Chapter 12-Differentiation.solution_text: $$\begin{aligned}y&=\sin x+\sin2x\\y'&=\frac{\pi}{180}\big(\cos x+2\cos2x\big)\\y''&=-\left(\frac{\pi}{180}\right)^2\big(\sin x+4\sin2x\big)\\y''=0&\Rightarrow \sin x+4\sin2x=0\\&\Rightarrow \sin x+8\sin x\cos x=0\\&\Rightarrow \sin x(1+8\cos x)=0\\\sin x=0&\Rightarrow x=0^\circ,180^\circ,360^\circ\\1+8\cos x=0&\Rightarrow \cos x=-\frac18\\x&=\cos^{-1}\!\left(-\frac18\right),\ 360^\circ-\cos^{-1}\!\left(-\frac18\right)\approx97.180^\circ,\ 262.820^\circ\\\text{(These give inflection when }y''\text{ changes sign.)}\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 12-Differentiation.question_text: For $y=\sin x+\sin3x$ (degrees), find stationary points in $0^\circ\le x\le360^\circ$.

Chapter 12-Differentiation.solution_text: $$\begin{aligned}y'&=\frac{\pi}{180}\cos x\\m_1m_2=-1&\Rightarrow \left(\frac{\pi}{180}\right)^2\cos x_1\cos x_2=-1\\\cos x_1\cos x_2&=-\left(\frac{180}{\pi}\right)^2\\\left|\cos x_1\cos x_2\right|\le1&\text{ but }\left(\frac{180}{\pi}\right)^2\approx3282>1\\\therefore\ &\text{No real solutions in degrees for this function.}\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 12-Differentiation.question_text: For $y=\cos x+2\sin x$ (degrees), find turning points in $0^\circ\le x\le360^\circ$ and the maximum value.
Chapter 12-Differentiation.hint: Set $y'=0\Rightarrow -\sin x+2\cos x=0\Rightarrow\tan x=2$, then compute $y$ and compare.
Chapter 12-Differentiation.solution_text: $$\begin{aligned}y&=\cos x+2\sin x\\y'&=\frac{\pi}{180}(-\sin x+2\cos x)\\y'=0&\Rightarrow \tan x=2\\x_1&=\tan^{-1}(2)\approx63.435^\circ,\ x_2=x_1+180^\circ\approx243.435^\circ\\\sin x_1&=\frac{2}{\sqrt5},\ \cos x_1=\frac{1}{\sqrt5}\\y(x_1)&=\frac{1}{\sqrt5}+2\cdot\frac{2}{\sqrt5}=\frac{5}{\sqrt5}=\sqrt5\\y(x_2)&=-\sqrt5\\\therefore\ \text{turning points: }(63.435^\circ,\sqrt5)&,\ (243.435^\circ,-\sqrt5),\ \max=\sqrt5\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 12-Differentiation.question_text: Let $y=\sin x+\cos x$ (degrees). Show that any stationary point satisfies $\sin x=\cos x$, and hence find the stationary points.
Chapter 12-Differentiation.hint: From $y'=0$ get $\cos x-\sin x=0$. Then solve in $[0,360]$.
Chapter 12-Differentiation.solution_text: $$\begin{aligned}y&=\sin x+\cos x\\y'&=\frac{\pi}{180}(\cos x-\sin x)\\y'=0&\Rightarrow \cos x-\sin x=0\Rightarrow \sin x=\cos x\\\tan x&=1\Rightarrow x=45^\circ,\ 225^\circ\\y(45^\circ)&=\sqrt2,\quad y(225^\circ)=-\sqrt2\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 12-Differentiation.question_text: For $y=\sin x+\cos x$ (degrees), find the tangent at $x=0^\circ$ and its $y$-intercept.

For $y=\tan x$ (degrees), find all stationary points in $0^\circ\le x\le360^\circ$ where defined.
Chapter 12-Differentiation.hint: $y'=\frac{\pi}{180}\sec^2x>0$ where defined, so no stationary points.
Chapter 12-Differentiation.solution_text: $$\begin{aligned}y&=\tan x\\y'&=\frac{\pi}{180}\sec^2x\\\sec^2x&>0\ \text{for all }x\text{ where }\tan x\text{ defined}\\\therefore\ y'&>0\ \text{everywhere in domain}\\\therefore\ &\text{no stationary points in }[0^\circ,360^\circ]\text{ (excluding }90^\circ,270^\circ)\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 12-Differentiation.question_text: Find $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\sin^2 x\right)$ for $x$ in degrees and evaluate at $x=45^\circ$.
Chapter 12-Differentiation.hint: Use chain rule: $d(\sin^2x)/dx=2\sin x\cdot d(\sin x)/dx$, with degree factor.

Chapter 12-Differentiation.question_text: For $y=\dfrac{\cos x}{1+\sin x}$ (degrees), find $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ in simplest form.
Chapter 12-Differentiation.hint: Use quotient rule and simplify; also note $\dfrac{\cos x}{1+\sin x}=\sec x-\tan x$.
Chapter 12-Differentiation.solution_text: $$\begin{aligned}y&=\frac{\cos x}{1+\sin x}\\\frac{dy}{dx}&=\frac{(-\frac{\pi}{180}\sin x)(1+\sin x)-\cos x(\frac{\pi}{180}\cos x)}{(1+\sin x)^2}\\&=-\frac{\pi}{180}\cdot\frac{\sin x(1+\sin x)+\cos^2x}{(1+\sin x)^2}\\&=-\frac{\pi}{180}\cdot\frac{\sin x+\sin^2x+\cos^2x}{(1+\sin x)^2}\\&=-\frac{\pi}{180}\cdot\frac{\sin x+1}{(1+\sin x)^2}\\&=-\frac{\pi}{180}\cdot\frac{1}{1+\sin x}\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 12-Differentiation.question_text: A square sheet of side $24$ cm has equal squares of side $x$ cut from each corner and is folded to form an open box. Find $x$ for maximum volume and the maximum volume.
A rectangle is inscribed in a semicircle of radius $R$. If the rectangle has half-width $x$ and height $y$, with $x^2+y^2=R^2$, find the maximum area of the rectangle in terms of $R$.
A cylindrical can with no top has volume $V_0$. Find $r$ and $h$ that minimise surface area $S=\pi r^2+2\pi rh$.
Chapter 12-Differentiation.hint: Use constraint $V_0=\pi r^2h\Rightarrow h=\frac{V_0}{\pi r^2}$, substitute into $S(r)$ then differentiate.
Chapter 12-Differentiation.solution_text: $$\begin{aligned}V_0&=\pi r^2h\Rightarrow h=\frac{V_0}{\pi r^2}\\S(r)&=\pi r^2+2\pi r\left(\frac{V_0}{\pi r^2}\right)=\pi r^2+\frac{2V_0}{r}\\S'(r)&=2\pi r-\frac{2V_0}{r^2}=0\\2\pi r&=\frac{2V_0}{r^2}\Rightarrow \pi r^3=V_0\\r&=\left(\frac{V_0}{\pi}\right)^{1/3},\quad h=\frac{V_0}{\pi r^2}=r\\\therefore\ h&=r\ \text{at minimum}\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 12-Differentiation.question_title: Optimisation: closed cylinder min surface (fixed volume)
Chapter 12-Differentiation.question_text: A closed cylinder has fixed volume $V_0$. Find the relation between $h$ and $r$ when the surface area $S=2\pi r^2+2\pi rh$ is minimum.
Chapter 12-Differentiation.solution_text: $$\begin{aligned}V_0&=\pi r^2h\Rightarrow h=\frac{V_0}{\pi r^2}\\S(r)&=2\pi r^2+2\pi r\left(\frac{V_0}{\pi r^2}\right)=2\pi r^2+\frac{2V_0}{r}\\S'(r)&=4\pi r-\frac{2V_0}{r^2}=0\\4\pi r^3&=2V_0\Rightarrow 2\pi r^3=V_0\\h&=\frac{V_0}{\pi r^2}=\frac{2\pi r^3}{\pi r^2}=2r\\\therefore\ h&=2r\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 12-Differentiation.question_title: Optimisation: max area isosceles triangle (fixed perimeter)
Chapter 12-Differentiation.question_text: An isosceles triangle has perimeter $P$. Find the maximum area and the side lengths when area is maximum.
Chapter 12-Differentiation.hint: Let equal sides $a,a$ and base $b=P-2a$. Height $h=\sqrt{a^2-(b/2)^2}$; maximise $A=\frac12bh$.
Chapter 12-Differentiation.solution_text: $$\begin{aligned}b&=P-2a\\h&=\sqrt{a^2-\left(\frac{b}{2}\right)^2}=\sqrt{a^2-\left(\frac{P-2a}{2}\right)^2}\\A(a)&=\frac12 b h=\frac12(P-2a)\sqrt{a^2-\left(\frac{P-2a}{2}\right)^2}\\\text{Max occurs at }a&=\frac{P}{3}\ (\text{equilateral case})\\\therefore\ a&=\frac{P}{3},\ b=\frac{P}{3},\ A_{\max}=\frac{\sqrt3}{36}P^2\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 12-Differentiation.question_title: Related rates: balloon with V(t) given
Chapter 12-Differentiation.question_text: A spherical balloon has volume $V=100t$ cm$^3$ at time $t$ seconds. Find $\frac{dr}{dt}$ when $t=8$.
Chapter 12-Differentiation.hint: Use $V=\frac43\pi r^3$ so $dV/dt=4\pi r^2\,dr/dt$; find $r$ at $t=8$.
Chapter 12-Differentiation.solution_text: $$\begin{aligned}V&=100t\Rightarrow \frac{dV}{dt}=100\\V&=\frac43\pi r^3\\\frac{dV}{dt}&=4\pi r^2\frac{dr}{dt}\\t=8:\ V&=800=\frac43\pi r^3\Rightarrow r^3=\frac{600}{\pi}\Rightarrow r=\left(\frac{600}{\pi}\right)^{1/3}\\\frac{dr}{dt}&=\frac{100}{4\pi r^2}=\frac{25}{\pi r^2}=\frac{25}{\pi\left(\frac{600}{\pi}\right)^{2/3}}=\frac{25}{\pi^{1/3}600^{2/3}}\ \text{cm s}^{-1}\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 12-Differentiation.question_title: Optimisation: min material for cone (fixed volume)
Chapter 12-Differentiation.question_text: A cone has fixed volume $V_0=\frac13\pi r^2h$. Find the relation between $h$ and $r$ that minimises the lateral surface area $S=\pi r\sqrt{r^2+h^2}$.
Chapter 12-Differentiation.hint: Express $h=\frac{3V_0}{\pi r^2}$, minimise $S(r)=\pi r\sqrt{r^2+h(r)^2}$ using derivative (use $S^2$).
Chapter 12-Differentiation.solution_text: $$\begin{aligned}V_0&=\frac13\pi r^2h\Rightarrow h=\frac{3V_0}{\pi r^2}\\S&=\pi r\sqrt{r^2+h^2}\Rightarrow S^2=\pi^2r^2(r^2+h^2)=\pi^2(r^4+r^2h^2)\\\text{Up to constant: }f(r)&=r^4+r^2h^2=r^4+r^2\left(\frac{3V_0}{\pi r^2}\right)^2=r^4+\frac{9V_0^2}{\pi^2}\cdot\frac{1}{r^2}\\f'(r)&=4r^3-\frac{18V_0^2}{\pi^2}\cdot\frac{1}{r^3}=0\\4r^6&=\frac{18V_0^2}{\pi^2}\Rightarrow r^6=\frac{9}{2}\frac{V_0^2}{\pi^2}\\\frac{h}{r}&=\frac{3V_0}{\pi r^3}=\sqrt{2}\ \Rightarrow h=\sqrt2\,r\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 12-Differentiation.question_title: Optimisation: max area of trapezium (fixed sides)
Chapter 12-Differentiation.question_text: An isosceles trapezium has parallel sides $a$ and $b$ with $a>b$, and equal non-parallel sides length $c$. Show the area is maximised when it is cyclic (right angles at one base) and find max area in terms of $a,b,c$ given feasibility.
Chapter 12-Differentiation.hint: Model height $h=\sqrt{c^2-\left(\frac{a-b}{2}\right)^2}$; area $A=\frac12(a+b)h$ is fixed by geometry, so “max” is achieved by symmetric placement.
Chapter 12-Differentiation.solution_text: $$\begin{aligned}\text{For isosceles trapezium: offset }d&=\frac{a-b}{2}\\h&=\sqrt{c^2-d^2}=\sqrt{c^2-\left(\frac{a-b}{2}\right)^2}\\A&=\frac12(a+b)h=\frac12(a+b)\sqrt{c^2-\left(\frac{a-b}{2}\right)^2}\\\text{This is the (unique) feasible area; }&\text{max occurs at symmetric configuration.}\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 12-Differentiation.question_title: Optimisation: min sum of perimeter and area

Chapter 12-Differentiation.question_text: Find and classify stationary points of $y=\sin x+\cos x$ for $0\le x\le2\pi$.
Chapter 12-Differentiation.hint: $y'=\cos x-\sin x=0\Rightarrow \tan x=1$; use $y''=-\sin x-\cos x$.
Chapter 12-Differentiation.solution_text: $$\begin{aligned}y&=\sin x+\cos x\\y'&=\cos x-\sin x=0\Rightarrow \tan x=1\\x&=\frac{\pi}{4},\ \frac{5\pi}{4}\\y''&=-\sin x-\cos x\\y''\!\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)&=-\sqrt2<0\Rightarrow \text{max}\\y''\!\left(\frac{5\pi}{4}\right)&=\sqrt2>0\Rightarrow \text{min}\\y\!\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\right)&=\sqrt2,\quad y\!\left(\frac{5\pi}{4}\right)=-\sqrt2\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 12-Differentiation.question_text: Find the least value of $f(x)=ax^{2}-12x+9$ for $a>0$, in terms of $a$.

Chapter 12-Differentiation.solution_text: $$\begin{aligned}y&=x^5-5x^3\\y'&=5x^4-15x^2=5x^2(x^2-3)\\y'=0&\Rightarrow x=0,\ \pm\sqrt3\\\text{Sign of }y':\ x^2\ge0&\Rightarrow \text{sign depends on }(x^2-3)\\|x|<\sqrt3&\Rightarrow y'<0,\quad |x|>\sqrt3\Rightarrow y'>0\\\therefore\ x=-\sqrt3&:\ +\to-\ \text{local max},\ x=\sqrt3:\ -\to+\ \text{local min}\\x=0&:\ y'\text{ does not change sign }\Rightarrow \text{stationary point of inflection}\\y(\pm\sqrt3)&=\pm(3\sqrt3)-5(\pm3\sqrt3)=\mp12\sqrt3,\quad y(0)=0\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 12-Differentiation.question_text: Find and classify stationary points of $y=x^{4}-2x^{2}+1$.

Chapter 12-Differentiation.solution_text: $$\begin{aligned}y&=\sin x+2\cos x\\y'&=\cos x-2\sin x=0\Rightarrow \tan x=\frac{1}{2}\\x&=\alpha,\ \alpha+\pi,\ \alpha=\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac12\right)\\y''&=-\sin x-2\cos x\\y''(\alpha)&=-\sin\alpha-2\cos\alpha<0\Rightarrow \text{max}\\y''(\alpha+\pi)&=-y''(\alpha)>0\Rightarrow \text{min}\\\text{Also }y_{\max}&=\sqrt{1^2+2^2}=\sqrt5,\ y_{\min}=-\sqrt5\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 12-Differentiation.question_text: Find and classify stationary points of $y=e^{x}(x^{2}-4x)$.
Find stationary points and classify for $y=\frac{x}{1+x^{2}}$.

Chapter 12-Differentiation.solution_text: $$\begin{aligned}y&=x^4-4x^3\\y'&=4x^3-12x^2=4x^2(x-3)\\y'=0&\Rightarrow x=0,\ 3\\y(0)&=0,\ y(3)=81-108=-27\\\text{Since }x^2\ge0,\ \text{sign}(y')&=\text{sign}(x-3)\ (\text{except }x=0)\\x=0&:\ y'\text{ negative on both sides}\Rightarrow \text{stationary inflection}\\x=3&:\ y'\ -\to+\Rightarrow \text{local minimum}\\\therefore&\ (0,0)\text{ stationary inflection},\ (3,-27)\text{ local min}\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 12-Differentiation.question_text: Find and classify stationary points of $y=x^2+\frac{9}{x}$ for $x\ne0$.
Show that $y=x+\frac{1}{x^2}$ has exactly one stationary point for $x>0$ and none for $x<0$. Find it and classify.
Chapter 12-Differentiation.hint: Solve $y'=1-2/x^3=0\Rightarrow x^3=2$; sign of $x^3$ gives existence.
Chapter 12-Differentiation.solution_text: $$\begin{aligned}y&=x+x^{-2}\\y'&=1-2x^{-3}\\y'=0&\Rightarrow x^3=2\Rightarrow x=\sqrt[3]{2}>0\\\text{If }x<0,\ x^3<0&\Rightarrow x^3=2\text{ impossible, so no stationary point}\\y''&=6x^{-4}>0\Rightarrow \text{local minimum at }x=\sqrt[3]{2}\\y\!\left(\sqrt[3]{2}\right)&=\sqrt[3]{2}+2^{-2/3}\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 12-Differentiation.question_text: For $y=\sin x+\sin 2x$ (degrees), find stationary points in $0^\circ\le x\le360^\circ$ and classify.
Chapter 12-Differentiation.hint: Convert derivative using $\frac{d}{dx}\sin(kx)=k\cos(kx)$ (degrees treated formally); solve $\cos x+2\cos2x=0$.
Chapter 12-Differentiation.solution_text: $$\begin{aligned}y&=\sin x+\sin2x\\y'&=\cos x+2\cos2x\\\cos2x&=2\cos^2x-1\\0&=\cos x+2(2\cos^2x-1)=\cos x+4\cos^2x-2\\4c^2+c-2&=0\ (c=\cos x)\\c&=\frac{-1\pm\sqrt{1+32}}{8}=\frac{-1\pm\sqrt{33}}{8}\\\text{Keep }c\in[-1,1]&\Rightarrow c_1=\frac{-1+\sqrt{33}}{8}\ (\approx0.593),\ c_2=\frac{-1-\sqrt{33}}{8}\ (\approx-0.843)\\x&=\cos^{-1}(c_1),\ 360^\circ-\cos^{-1}(c_1),\ \cos^{-1}(c_2),\ 360^\circ-\cos^{-1}(c_2)\\\text{Classify via }y''&=-\sin x-4\sin2x\ \text{(substitute each)}\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 12-Differentiation.question_text: Find and classify stationary points of $y=3\sin x-4\cos x$ for $0\le x\le2\pi$.
Chapter 12-Differentiation.solution_text: $$\begin{aligned}y&=3\sin x-4\cos x\\y'&=3\cos x+4\sin x=0\Rightarrow \tan x=-\frac{3}{4}\\\text{Let }\beta&=\tan^{-1}\!\left(\frac{3}{4}\right)\\\tan x<0&\Rightarrow x=\pi-\beta,\ 2\pi-\beta\\y''&=-3\sin x+4\cos x\\y''(\pi-\beta)&<0\Rightarrow \text{local max},\quad y''(2\pi-\beta)>0\Rightarrow \text{local min}\\\text{Also }y_{\max}&=5,\ y_{\min}=-5\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 12-Differentiation.question_text: Find and classify stationary points of $y=e^{-x}(x^2+1)$.
Chapter 12-Differentiation.hint: Solve $y'=0$ using product rule, factor out $e^{-x}$.
Chapter 12-Differentiation.solution_text: $$\begin{aligned}y&=e^{-x}(x^2+1)\\y'&=-e^{-x}(x^2+1)+e^{-x}(2x)=e^{-x}(-x^2+2x-1)\\y'=0&\Rightarrow -x^2+2x-1=0\Rightarrow (x-1)^2=0\Rightarrow x=1\\y''&=\frac{d}{dx}\big(e^{-x}(-(x-1)^2)\big)=e^{-x}(x-1)^2-2e^{-x}(x-1)\\y''(1)&=0\ \text{and sign changes?}\\\text{Since }y'&=-e^{-x}(x-1)^2\le0\text{ with equality only at }1,\ \text{so }y\text{ has stationary inflection at }x=1\\y(1)&=e^{-1}(2)=\frac{2}{e}\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 12-Differentiation.question_text: Find and classify stationary points of $y=\ln x-x^2$ for $x>0$.
Let $y=x|x-2|$. Find all stationary points and classify.
Chapter 12-Differentiation.hint: Split into $x\ge2$ and $x<2$, differentiate each piece and check join at $x=2$.
Chapter 12-Differentiation.solution_text: $$\begin{aligned}y&=x|x-2|=\begin{cases}x(x-2)=x^2-2x,&x\ge2\\x(2-x)=2x-x^2,&x<2\end{cases}\\y'&=\begin{cases}2x-2,&x\ge2\\2-2x,&x<2\end{cases}\\x\ge2:\ 2x-2=0&\Rightarrow x=1\ (\text{not allowed})\\x<2:\ 2-2x=0&\Rightarrow x=1\ (\text{allowed})\\\therefore\ \text{stationary at }x=1,\ y(1)&=1| -1|=1\\\text{At }x=2,\ y'\text{ left}=-2,\ y'\text{ right}=2&\Rightarrow \text{corner, not stationary}\\\text{Since }y'\ +\to- \text{ at }x=1&\Rightarrow \text{local max at }(1,1)\end{aligned}$$

Chapter 12-Differentiation.question_text: For $y=x^4-2ax^2$, find stationary points in terms of $a$ and classify (assume $a>0$).
Chapter 12-Differentiation.solution_text: $$\begin{aligned}y&=x^4-2ax^2,\ a>0\\y'&=4x^3-4ax=4x(x^2-a)\\y'=0&\Rightarrow x=0,\ \pm\sqrt{a}\\y''&=12x^2-4a\\y''(0)&=-4a<0\Rightarrow \text{local max}\\y''(\pm\sqrt a)&=12a-4a=8a>0\Rightarrow \text{local mins}\\y(0)&=0,\quad y(\pm\sqrt a)=a^2-2a\cdot a=-a^2\end{aligned}$$
